opus-5.5.text:
I think what draws me most is that it changes the question you're asking. For a long time, the way we solved hard problems, whether in vision, robotics, or anything involving the physical world, was to sit down and try to write the rules ourselves. You'd think very carefully about how an object looks, how light bounces, how a hand should grasp something, and you'd encode that knowledge by hand. And it works up to a point, but the world is just so much richer and messier than anything you can write down.

Data-driven learning flips that around. Instead of asking "how do I describe the solution?", you ask "what experience would let a system discover the solution itself?" That shift is really powerful, because the real world has a long tail of situations no engineer would ever anticipate, and data is the only thing that can cover that tail. When you watch a model pick up some regularity you never explicitly told it about, it's honestly a bit magical. It feels less like programming and more like teaching.

There's also something I find intellectually honest about it. Data keeps you grounded. You can have a beautiful theory, but if it doesn't hold up on real examples, the data tells you right away. So it becomes this loop of building something, seeing where it fails, and asking what information is missing. That's a very satisfying way to make progress.

And I think, looking at the last decade, the evidence is pretty clear: every time we've given these systems more and better data, along with the right structure to learn from it, they've surprised us. So for me it's not just a technique. It's a bet that the most general way to build intelligent systems is to let them learn from the world, and our job as researchers is to figure out what data, what structure, and what objectives make that learning work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, what draws me to it is that it's a kind of humility built into the method. For a long time, the way we solved hard problems was that a very smart person would sit down and try to write out the rules: this is how language works, this is what a cat looks like, this is how a car should decide to brake. And every time, the rules turned out to be incomplete. The world is just messier than any one person's description of it.

Data-driven learning flips that around. Instead of saying "I know how this works, let me encode it," you say "I don't fully know how this works, but I have a lot of examples, and I'm going to let the structure in those examples speak." That's very freeing. It means the ceiling on what you can solve isn't your own ability to articulate a solution. It's the quality and scale of the evidence you can gather, and how well you can set up the learning problem.

The second thing that pulls me in is the feedback loop. In traditional engineering you build something, it either works or it doesn't, and then you reason about why. In machine learning you get to run that loop hundreds of times. Change the data, change the objective, change the architecture, measure, repeat. It makes the work feel almost experimental, closer to science than to pure construction. You form a hypothesis about what the model needs and the data tells you very quickly whether you were right.

And I'll admit there's an aesthetic pull too. When you see a system pick up a behavior you never explicitly programmed, that moment when it generalizes to something you didn't anticipate, it's genuinely surprising. Not in a mystical way, there's always a reason underneath, but it reminds you that there's more regularity in the world than we tend to assume, and that if you're patient and careful, you can let it surface on its own.

So I'd say it's a combination: a healthier relationship with my own ignorance, a fast loop for being wrong and correcting, and the occasional delight of being surprised by something you built.

astra-6.text: What draws me to it is the ability to learn from examples when it’s difficult to write down all the rules. You can start with a problem, look for patterns in the data, and test whether those patterns actually help you make better predictions or decisions. I find that cycle of learning and testing really appealing. And it pushes you to ask good questions: What does the data capture? What’s missing? Are we measuring something that matters? For me, that combination of experimentation and practical problem-solving is the attraction.
